raw_findings.message: Casting minted shares to uint128 truncates positions above 2^128−1 while `totalShares` still records the full amount, so a large deposit leaves the user unable to withdraw the shares recorded in the vault.

Every deposit appends another holder entry and `distributeRewards` iterates over the entire array, so users can grow it until reward distribution exceeds the transaction gas limit and becomes unusable.
`sharePrice()` divides by `totalShares` without handling an empty vault, so calling it before the first deposit reverts.
Withdrawal makes external calls before reducing the caller's shares or total shares, allowing a recipient that reenters during a payout to withdraw repeatedly against the unchanged position.
Dividing the reward amount by `totalShares` before multiplying by positions rounds small rewards to zero and leaves the supplied ETH uncredited as rewards.
Because each deposit adds another entry for the same address, this loop credits that address's full position repeatedly, potentially making `rewardsOwed` exceed the ETH available for rewards.
Anyone can change `feeRecipient`, so an attacker can redirect fees from later withdrawals to an address they control.
Checking `tx.origin` instead of `msg.sender` lets a contract called by the owner change the fee, so an owner can be tricked into invoking a malicious intermediary that sets the fee.
During a deposit, `totalAssets()` already includes the incoming ETH, so the deposit is included in its own pricing denominator and mints too few shares, potentially zeroing a depositor's shares.
The fee transfer's success flag is ignored, so if `feeRecipient` rejects ETH the withdrawal still succeeds and the unpaid fee remains in the vault instead of reaching the recipient.
Unchecked subtraction wraps an insufficient allowance to a huge value, allowing an unapproved spender to transfer tokens from an account that has enough balance.

raw_findings.message: Casting `shares` to `uint128` truncates deposits above `type(uint128).max` while `totalShares` is increased by the full amount, leaving the depositor unable to withdraw their recorded share of the assets.

Every deposit appends another entry for the same address, so `distributeRewards` credits that holder once per entry and can make `rewardsOwed` exceed the vault balance, breaking asset accounting and withdrawals.
Repeated deposits grow `holders` without bound, and the distribution loop processes every entry, allowing an attacker to make owner reward distributions run out of gas.
`sharePrice()` divides by `totalShares`, so it panics before the first deposit and again after all shares are withdrawn.
Withdrawal makes external calls before reducing the caller's shares or clearing rewards, allowing a recipient or fee recipient to reenter and withdraw against stale state.
Dividing the reward amount before allocating it rounds small distributions down to zero or leaves a remainder uncredited, so sent rewards instead remain in the vault as share backing.
Anyone can change `feeRecipient`, allowing an attacker to redirect future withdrawal fees to an address they control.

Using `tx.origin` for authorization lets an intermediary contract change the fee when the owner is tricked into calling it, and prevents a contract owner from acting unless its origin is separately the owner.
During a payable deposit, `totalAssets()` already includes `msg.value`, so the new deposit is priced against assets that include itself and subsequent depositors receive too few shares.

With no virtual shares or minimum-share check, an attacker can seed the vault with a tiny deposit and donate ETH until a victim's deposit rounds to zero shares, then withdraw the victim's contribution.
The fee transfer's success flag is ignored, so a rejecting fee recipient can prevent the fee from being paid while the withdrawal proceeds as if it had been.
Unchecked allowance subtraction wraps when `transferFrom` is called without sufficient approval, allowing tokens to be transferred and leaving the spender with a huge allowance.

raw_findings.message: Casting minted shares to uint128 truncates deposits above the type limit while totalShares records the full amount, leaving shares unwithdrawable and corrupting ownership accounting.
sharePrice divides by totalShares without handling an empty vault, so calling it before any shares exist or after the vault is emptied reverts.
The vault pays the withdrawing user before reducing their shares or clearing rewards, allowing a reentrant receiver to withdraw against the same position and claim more than its entitlement.
distributeRewards divides by totalShares without checking for an empty vault, so an owner call before any deposits reverts.

Dividing the reward amount by totalShares before multiplying truncates fractional per-share rewards; when msg.value is less than totalShares, no rewards are credited and the funds instead become share backing.
Reward distribution iterates over every historical holder entry, so enough deposits can make the loop exceed the block gas limit and permanently prevent reward distributions.
Because each deposit appends another holder entry, repeat depositors are credited their full balance multiple times; this can make rewardsOwed exceed the ETH held and cause totalAssets to underflow.
setFeeRecipient has no owner check, so any caller can redirect future withdrawal fees to an address they control.
Using tx.origin for authorization lets an owner EOA be tricked into changing the fee through an intermediary contract and prevents contract-based owners from authorizing the call normally.
The fee transfer's return value is ignored, so a rejecting fee recipient leaves the fee in the vault while the withdrawal proceeds as if it was paid.
Unchecked allowance subtraction wraps when transferFrom is called without sufficient approval, allowing a caller with no allowance to transfer tokens from any sufficiently funded account.

fixed_raw_findings.message: The share calculation has no virtual shares or other protection against donation-driven price manipulation, so an attacker can make a victim's deposit mint very few shares and then withdraw nearly all of the victim's ETH.

This reserves rewards using aggregate shares even when per-holder rounding makes the sum claimable smaller; for example, three holders with 1 gwei of shares each and a 4 wei reward leave 1 wei permanently excluded from totalAssets after they claim.
Replacing a nonzero allowance lets a spender front-run the approval and spend the old allowance before the new one takes effect, potentially consuming both amounts.
Transfers accept the zero address as a recipient, permanently locking tokens while reporting success; mint also permits this destination at line 32.
